Getting started with panglm

Source: vignettes/panglm-intro.Rmd
panglm-intro.Rmd

This vignette covers the basic workflow of panglm: how panel data are laid out, the four classical estimators (pooled, fixed effects, between, random effects) and the correlated random effects compromise, how to choose between them, which standard errors to report, and how to get average partial effects, predictions, tables and plots. The other vignettes build on it:

  • vignette("panglm-outcomes"): counts, costs, bounded and censored outcomes;
  • vignette("panglm-endogeneity"): instrumental variables, Hausman-Taylor, dynamic GMM and sample selection;
  • vignette("panglm-policy"): difference-in-differences, event studies and staggered adoption;
  • vignette("panglm-heterogeneity"): random slopes, latent classes and quantile regression;
  • vignette("panglm-methods"): the technical reference.

Which estimator to start from:

Question Estimator model =
Effect of a change within a patient, robust to stable confounders fixed effects "within"
Effect of time-invariant traits (sex, treatment arm) random effects "random"
Within effects and time-invariant traits in one model correlated random effects "random", cre = TRUE
Differences between patients only between "between"
Descriptive population average, no panel structure pooled, cluster SE "pooling"

Data layout

panglm works with data in long format: one row per individual and period. The index argument names the individual and the time columns. Panels may be unbalanced; missing or duplicated index pairs are errors. The package ships a small synthetic panel of 60 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) seen at 5 visits.

library(panglm)
data(copd)
head(copd)
#>   id visit treatment age smoker  bmi crp fev1 exacerbations hospitalized
#> 1  1     1         1  70      0 28.5 5.9 2.61             2            0
#> 2  1     2         1  70      0 28.5 0.1 3.19             3            0
#> 3  1     3         1  70      0 28.5 4.1 2.88             5            1
#> 4  1     4         1  70      0 28.5 5.1 3.12             1            0
#> 5  1     5         1  70      0 28.5 3.3 2.91             3            0
#> 6  2     1         1  64      0 24.0 4.2 2.81             0            0

treatment, age, smoker and bmi are fixed at baseline; C-reactive protein (crp) changes from visit to visit. The outcomes are lung function (fev1, litres), the number of exacerbations and a hospital admission indicator.

The four estimators

Write the model as yit=xit𝖳β+αi+εity_{it} = x_{it}^{\mathsf T}\beta + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it}, where αi\alpha_i is the unobserved, stable part of a patient’s health.

Pooled least squares ignores αi\alpha_i. It is consistent only if αi\alpha_i is unrelated to the regressors, and its classical standard errors are wrong because the errors of one patient are correlated, so always cluster by individual.

fit_pool <- panglm(fev1 ~ treatment + age + smoker + crp, data = copd,
                   index = c("id", "visit"), model = "pooling",
                   vcov = "cluster")
summary(fit_pool)
#> 
#> Call:
#> panglm(formula = fev1 ~ treatment + age + smoker + crp, data = copd, 
#>     index = c("id", "visit"), model = "pooling", vcov = "cluster")
#> 
#> Family: gaussian  Link: identity  Model: pooling  Effect: individual 
#> N = 300  groups = 60  vcov: cluster 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  4.091479   0.454502   9.002  < 2e-16 ***
#> treatment    0.208556   0.112802   1.849  0.06448 .  
#> age         -0.014239   0.006661  -2.138  0.03254 *  
#> smoker      -0.355207   0.116640  -3.045  0.00232 ** 
#> crp         -0.032895   0.013675  -2.405  0.01615 *  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -189.6 
#> Dispersion parameter: 0.2107 
#> Residual df: 295  Iterations: 2

Fixed effects (the within estimator) removes αi\alpha_i by subtracting each patient’s mean. It uses only changes within a patient, so it is robust to any stable confounder, but time-invariant regressors are not identified and are dropped.

fit_fe <- panglm(fev1 ~ crp, data = copd, index = c("id", "visit"),
                 model = "within", vcov = "cluster")
summary(fit_fe)
#> 
#> Call:
#> panglm(formula = fev1 ~ crp, data = copd, index = c("id", "visit"), 
#>     model = "within", vcov = "cluster")
#> 
#> Family: gaussian  Link: identity  Model: within  Effect: individual 
#> N = 300  groups = 60  vcov: cluster 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>      Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> crp -0.035305   0.006072  -5.815 6.08e-09 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: 107.6 
#> Dispersion parameter: 0.03588 
#> Residual df: 239  Iterations: 2

A rise of 1 mg/L in CRP within a patient goes with a fall of about 35 mL in FEV1. effect = "twoways" adds visit effects, which absorb shocks common to all patients at a visit.

Between is least squares on the patient means, one row per patient. It uses only the differences between patients and is mostly useful as a contrast with the within estimator.

fit_be <- panglm(fev1 ~ crp + age, data = copd, index = c("id", "visit"),
                 model = "between")
coef(fit_be)
#> (Intercept)         crp         age 
#>  4.48547472 -0.05542943 -0.01932395

Random effects treats αi\alpha_i as a random draw, independent of the regressors (Swamy-Arora feasible GLS for the Gaussian model). It keeps the time-invariant regressors and is efficient when that independence holds.

fit_re <- panglm(fev1 ~ treatment + age + smoker + crp, data = copd,
                 index = c("id", "visit"), model = "random")
coef(fit_re)
#> (Intercept)   treatment         age      smoker         crp 
#>  4.10943890  0.20549733 -0.01430869 -0.35583462 -0.03519775

Correlated random effects (Mundlak 1978; Chamberlain 1980) lets αi\alpha_i depend on the patient means of the time-varying regressors, αi=x‾i𝖳γ+ai\alpha_i = \bar x_i^{\mathsf T}\gamma + a_i. With cre = TRUE these means enter as mean_<variable>. The slope of crp is then the within slope, while treatment, age and smoker stay in the model.

fit_cre <- panglm(fev1 ~ treatment + age + smoker + crp, data = copd,
                  index = c("id", "visit"), model = "random", cre = TRUE,
                  vcov = "cluster")
summary(fit_cre)
#> 
#> Call:
#> panglm(formula = fev1 ~ treatment + age + smoker + crp, data = copd, 
#>     index = c("id", "visit"), model = "random", vcov = "cluster", 
#>     cre = TRUE)
#> 
#> Family: gaussian  Link: identity  Model: random  Effect: individual 
#> N = 300  groups = 60  vcov: cluster 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)  4.004113   0.725081   5.522 3.35e-08 ***
#> treatment    0.223437   0.152615   1.464  0.14318    
#> age         -0.013902   0.007074  -1.965  0.04940 *  
#> smoker      -0.352154   0.116349  -3.027  0.00247 ** 
#> crp         -0.035305   0.006072  -5.815 6.08e-09 ***
#> mean_crp     0.013612   0.067007   0.203  0.83902    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -22.56 
#> Dispersion parameter: 0.0359 
#> Mundlak test (individual means jointly zero): chi2(1) = 0.04127, p = 0.839
#> Residual df: 294  Iterations: 2

Choosing between fixed and random effects

The Hausman (1978) test compares the fixed- and random-effects slopes. Under its null both are consistent and random effects is efficient. The classical version uses model-based covariances; the Mundlak form tests γ=0\gamma = 0 in the correlated random effects regression with a cluster-robust covariance, and stays valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, so it is the one to report.

fit_re1 <- panglm(fev1 ~ crp, data = copd, index = c("id", "visit"),
                  model = "random")
panhausman(fit_fe, fit_re1)
#> 
#>  Hausman specification test (fixed vs. random effects)
#> 
#> chisq = 0.08488 , df = 1 , p-value = 0.7708 
#> alternative hypothesis: one model is inconsistent
panhausman(fit_fe, method = "mundlak", data = copd)
#> 
#>  Mundlak specification test (fixed vs. random effects), vcov: cluster 
#> 
#> F = 0.1647 , df = 1, 59 , p-value = 0.6864 
#> alternative hypothesis: one model is inconsistent

Neither test rejects: in these data CRP is unrelated to the stable part of lung function, and random effects is acceptable. When the test rejects, use fixed effects, or correlated random effects if time-invariant regressors matter.

Standard errors

Every fit stores one covariance, chosen with vcov, and vcov() recomputes another one after fitting:

  • "classical": model based, valid only under the full model assumptions;
  • "HC1": robust to heteroskedasticity (pooled and fixed effects);
  • "cluster": robust to heteroskedasticity and to any correlation within an individual. This is the default choice for panel data (Cameron and Miller 2015). The cluster is the individual unless cluster gives a coarser grouping, such as the hospital.
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_fe, type = "classical")))
#>         crp 
#> 0.005974855
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_fe, type = "cluster")))
#>         crp 
#> 0.006071829
confint(fit_fe)
#>           2.5 %      97.5 %
#> crp -0.04720538 -0.02340425

Nonlinear models and average partial effects

The same interface fits binary, count and other nonlinear models through family. Their coefficients are on the link scale. partialeffects() reports average partial effects on the outcome scale: the mean derivative for continuous regressors and the mean discrete change for binary ones, with delta-method standard errors from the stored covariance. For random-effects models the mean integrates over the random intercept, which gives the average structural function of Wooldridge (2005).

fit_hosp <- panglm(hospitalized ~ treatment + age + crp, data = copd,
                   index = c("id", "visit"), model = "random",
                   family = "probit", cre = TRUE, vcov = "cluster")
partialeffects(fit_hosp)
#> 
#> Average partial effects
#> Delta-method standard errors, vcov: cluster 
#> 
#>       term contrast estimate std.error statistic   p.value  conf.low conf.high
#>  treatment    1 - 0 -0.13560  0.069090    -1.963 0.0496700 -0.271000 -0.000194
#>        age    dY/dX  0.01161  0.003145     3.691 0.0002238  0.005442  0.017770
#>        crp    dY/dX  0.01713  0.013290     1.289 0.1974000 -0.008917  0.043180

Active treatment lowers the probability of an admission between visits by about 14 percentage points, and each extra year of age raises it by about 1 point.

Predictions

predict() returns the linear predictor (type = "link") or the mean (type = "response"), in sample or for new data. Random-effects predictions are population averages. Fixed-effects predictions add the estimated individual effect, so newdata needs the index columns; an unseen individual is an error unless allow.new.levels = TRUE, which sets its effect to zero.

new <- data.frame(id = 1, visit = 6, treatment = c(0, 1), age = 65,
                  smoker = 0, crp = 3)
predict(fit_re, newdata = new, type = "response")
#> [1] 3.073780 3.279278
predict(fit_fe, newdata = data.frame(id = 1:2, visit = 6, crp = 3))
#> [1] 2.966713 2.905419

Tables

tidy() and glance() methods (from the generics package) exist for every model class, so the fits work with broom and modelsummary.

generics::tidy(fit_fe, conf.int = TRUE)
#>   term    estimate   std.error statistic      p.value    conf.low   conf.high
#> 1  crp -0.03530482 0.006071829 -5.814528 6.080537e-09 -0.04720538 -0.02340425
generics::glance(fit_fe)
#>    model     effect   family     link vcov.type   logLik       AIC      BIC
#> 1 within individual gaussian identity   cluster 107.5641 -91.12812 138.5064
#>   df.logLik df.residual r.squared adj.r.squared nobs n.groups theta
#> 1        62         239 0.8954046     0.8691464  300       60    NA
modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list(Pooled = fit_pool, "Fixed effects" = fit_fe, "Random effects" = fit_re),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "n.groups"), output = "markdown"
)
Pooled Fixed effects Random effects
(Intercept) 4.091 4.109
(0.455) (0.434)
treatment 0.209 0.205
(0.113) (0.116)
age -0.014 -0.014
(0.007) (0.007)

Plots

plot() draws the coefficients with confidence intervals, the residuals against fitted values, or observed against fitted values.

plot(fit_cre, which = "coefficients")

plot(fit_fe, which = "residuals")

Validated against

The pooled, within, between and random-effects Gaussian estimators reproduce plm::plm(); cluster and HC1 covariances reproduce plm::vcovHC() and sandwich; pooled GLMs reproduce stats::glm(); random-intercept GLMs reproduce lme4 and glmmTMB; average partial effects reproduce marginaleffects. The scripts are in the package source (tests/testthat and validation/).

References

Cameron, A. C., and Miller, D. L. (2015). A practitioner’s guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources, 50, 317-372.

Chamberlain, G. (1980). Analysis of covariance with qualitative data. Review of Economic Studies, 47, 225-238.

Croissant, Y., and Millo, G. (2008). Panel data econometrics in R: the plm package. Journal of Statistical Software, 27(2), 1-43.

Hausman, J. A. (1978). Specification tests in econometrics. Econometrica, 46, 1251-1271.

Mundlak, Y. (1978). On the pooling of time series and cross section data. Econometrica, 46, 69-85.

Swamy, P. A. V. B., and Arora, S. S. (1972). The exact finite sample properties of the estimators of coefficients in the error components regression models. Econometrica, 40, 261-275.

Wooldridge, J. M. (2005). Unobserved heterogeneity and estimation of average partial effects. In D. W. K. Andrews and J. H. Stock (Eds.), Identification and Inference for Econometric Models, 27-55. Cambridge University Press.

Wooldridge, J. M. (2010). Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, 2nd edition. MIT Press.
